content: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis (EIA) is a medical condition characterized by the onset of anaphylaxis symptoms triggered by physical exercise. In certain cases, individuals experience anaphylaxis only when physical activity occurs in conjunction with exposure to a specific triggering agent shortly after its ingestion. For these individuals, neither exercise alone nor the ingestion of the triggering agent alone is sufficient to provoke anaphylaxis. Common triggers include specific foods such as celery, wheat, soy protein, cheese, and shellfish, as well as medications like aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). However, in other cases, individuals may develop anaphylaxis solely due to exercise, without any identifiable triggering agent. Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA) is a specific subtype of EIA that results from an IgE-mediated allergic reaction to the omega-gliadin component of wheat gluten. This reaction may also involve homologous proteins found in certain subspecies of Aegilopides speltoides (genome BB). WDEIA shares similarities with baker's asthma, another IgE-mediated condition. However, neither WDEIA nor baker's asthma is necessarily associated with gluten intolerance, despite their involvement of the IgE subclass of immunoglobulins. Unlike gluten sensitivity, WDEIA does not appear to extend to gluten found in rye or barley. In patients with WDEIA, IgE antibodies specifically recognize the omega-gliadin (Gli-B1) gene product located on chromosome 1B of wheat. Additionally, the immune responses observed in patients with wheat-dependent urticaria seem to parallel those seen in WDEIA.
